missions.title: The Book That Shows the Way

ayahs.meaning: Alif, Lam, Mim: opening letters whose ultimate meaning Allah knows best.

ayahs.arabic: تِلْكَ ءَايَـٰتُ ٱلْكِتَـٰبِ ٱلْحَكِيمِ  ﴿2﴾
ayahs.meaning: These are verses of the Book characterized by wisdom.

ayahs.arabic: هُدًى وَرَحْمَةً لِّلْمُحْسِنِينَ  ﴿3﴾
ayahs.meaning: The Book is guidance and mercy for those who strive to do good.

ayahs.arabic: ٱلَّذِينَ يُقِيمُونَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَيُؤْتُونَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَهُم بِٱلْءَاخِرَةِ هُمْ يُوقِنُونَ  ﴿4﴾
ayahs.meaning: The doers of good establish Salah, give Zakah, and are certain of the Hereafter.

ayahs.arabic: أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ عَلَىٰ هُدًى مِّن رَّبِّهِمْ ۖ وَأُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْمُفْلِحُونَ  ﴿5﴾
ayahs.meaning: Such people follow guidance from their Lord and are truly successful.

options: Collecting awards while ignoring duties.
Following Allah’s guidance through Salah and good deeds.
Doing kind acts only when others can see.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:1–5  |  CORE TRAITS: Qur’an • Guidance • Salah • Good deeds
missions.aim: Understand that divine guidance is a mercy and that real success joins belief with worship and good deeds.
missions.tafsir: The surah opens with the disjointed letters Alif–Lam–Mim; their ultimate significance is known to Allah. It then describes the Qur’an as a wise Book and guidance and mercy for the muhsinin, people devoted to doing good. The next verses identify practical marks of their life: they establish prayer, give Zakah and firmly believe in the Hereafter. Classical Tafsir stresses that true success is not merely winning a contest, gathering possessions or appearing admired. It comes from following Allah’s guidance with belief and righteous action. Zakah is an established act of worship with its own legal rules; a child’s small gift is a preparatory exercise in generosity, not a substitute for the obligatory Zakah owed by an eligible adult. The passage sets the foundation for everything Luqman will later teach: wisdom begins when the heart accepts guidance and the hands learn to do good.
missions.story: Akhlaq stared at the school achievement board. It displayed medals for science, sports and drawing. “I wish my name were there,” he told Imaan. She agreed that trying hard at school was good, but asked whether a medal was the only kind of success. That afternoon they visited Dadi Jaan, who needed help organizing books. Akhlaq sorted the shelves and noticed how pleased she was. Later Sheikh Uncle read the opening verses of Surah Luqman. He explained that Allah’s guidance helps believers connect their prayers, their kindness and their hope in the Hereafter. Akhlaq still wanted to earn a medal, but he made a new goal as well: to become someone whose good deeds were not limited to moments when others were watching.
missions.question: What is the strongest picture of success for a believer?
missions.feedback: Well done. Allah’s guidance shapes both worship and everyday goodness.
missions.action: Offer one small helpful act at home today, even if no one gives you a prize.
missions.reflection: What good deed matters even when nobody applauds?
missions.vocabulary: Muhsin — person who strives to do good; Falah — lasting success
missions.careNote: Do not claim every child is legally responsible for Zakah; preserve the original worship meaning. Explain opening letters without speculative certainty.
missions.next: Next, the surah contrasts listening to guidance with deliberately pushing it away.
missions.review: Circle one action in a fictional school day that reflects worship, one that reflects kindness, and one that reflects hope in Allah.

missions.title: Choose What Deserves Your Attention

ayahs.arabic: وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يَشْتَرِى لَهْوَ ٱلْحَدِيثِ لِيُضِلَّ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ وَيَتَّخِذَهَا هُزُوًا ۚ أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ مُّهِينٌ  ﴿6﴾
ayahs.meaning: Some deliberately choose distracting, misleading talk to turn others away from Allah’s path and mock it; the verse warns of the consequence.

ayahs.arabic: وَإِذَا تُتْلَىٰ عَلَيْهِ ءَايَـٰتُنَا وَلَّىٰ مُسْتَكْبِرًا كَأَن لَّمْ يَسْمَعْهَا كَأَنَّ فِىٓ أُذُنَيْهِ وَقْرًا ۖ فَبَشِّرْهُ بِعَذَابٍ أَلِيمٍ  ﴿7﴾
ayahs.meaning: When Allah’s verses are recited to such a person, he proudly turns away as though he had not heard; a painful consequence is warned of.

options: Share it so friends laugh.
Stop watching and choose respectful, beneficial content.
Conclude that every kind of play is forbidden.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:6–7  |  CORE TRAITS: Truthfulness • Attention • Respect for revelation
missions.aim: Recognize harmful distraction and mockery without assuming that all lawful play is forbidden.
missions.tafsir: Verses 6–7 warn of lahw al-hadith used to mislead people away from Allah’s path, ridiculing revelation, and arrogantly refusing to listen. Early commentators, including Ibn Mas‘ud in reports cited by Ibn Kathir, discussed singing in connection with lahw al-hadith; al-Tabari also explained the broad meaning of speech that diverts people from Allah’s way. This is a serious discussion of misleading or distracting entertainment, not a licence to tell children that every game, smile or permitted recreation is sinful. The words “to mislead” and “to mock” are integral to the verse’s warning. For a child, the safest initial application is learning to notice when a video, joke or group chat begins to disrespect faith, encourage cruelty or swallow time meant for worship and responsibilities. The point is to honour revelation, not to turn a disputed entertainment ruling into a multiple-choice doctrinal trap.
missions.story: Akhlaq opened a stream of funny clips after finishing homework. At first the jokes were harmless. Then one clip began making disrespectful fun of someone’s prayer, and the next invited viewers to send cruel comments. He felt uncomfortable but kept watching because all his friends were sharing it. Imaan noticed his worried expression. “We can choose something better,” she said. They closed the videos and found an animal documentary they both enjoyed. At their evening lesson, Sheikh Uncle read the verses about harmful distractions and pride toward Allah’s words. He reminded them that play can have a proper place, but mocking religion or hurting people is never entertainment. Akhlaq decided to pay attention not only to how amusing something looked but also to where it was leading his heart.
missions.question: A video begins mocking prayer and encouraging hurtful comments. What should Akhlaq do?
missions.feedback: You can enjoy appropriate recreation without supporting mockery or harm.
missions.action: Turn away from one unkind or disrespectful clip or conversation today.
missions.reflection: What helps me notice when entertainment becomes harmful?
missions.vocabulary: Lahw al-hadith — distracting speech or amusement; Istikbar — arrogance
missions.careNote: Preserve historical exegetical discussions on singing/music in parent notes; do not flatten different juristic details or imply every game is unlawful.
missions.next: Faith also holds out hope and invites us to notice Allah’s creation.
missions.review: Choose between three fictional media clips and explain which should be closed and why.

missions.title: A World Full of Signs

ayahs.arabic: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّـٰلِحَـٰتِ لَهُمْ جَنَّـٰتُ ٱلنَّعِيمِ  ﴿8﴾
ayahs.meaning: Those who believe and do righteous deeds are promised gardens of delight.

ayahs.arabic: خَـٰلِدِينَ فِيهَا ۖ وَعْدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقًّا ۚ وَهُوَ ٱلْعَزِيزُ ٱلْحَكِيمُ  ﴿9﴾
ayahs.meaning: They will remain there by Allah’s true promise; He is Mighty and Wise.

ayahs.arabic: خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ بِغَيْرِ عَمَدٍ تَرَوْنَهَا ۖ وَأَلْقَىٰ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ رَوَٰسِىَ أَن تَمِيدَ بِكُمْ وَبَثَّ فِيهَا مِن كُلِّ دَآبَّةٍ ۚ وَأَنزَلْنَا مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ مَآءً فَأَنۢبَتْنَا فِيهَا مِن كُلِّ زَوْجٍ كَرِيمٍ  ﴿10﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah made the heavens, established the mountains, spread living creatures, and sent rain that brings forth good plants.

ayahs.arabic: هَـٰذَا خَلْقُ ٱللَّهِ فَأَرُونِى مَاذَا خَلَقَ ٱلَّذِينَ مِن دُونِهِۦ ۚ بَلِ ٱلظَّـٰلِمُونَ فِى ضَلَـٰلٍ مُّبِينٍ  ﴿11﴾
ayahs.meaning: This is Allah’s creation: the verse challenges claims that beings worshipped besides Him created anything comparable.

options: That the natural world needs no Creator.
That Allah creates and provides, and that we should be grateful.
That we can know everything about the universe already.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:8–11  |  CORE TRAITS: Tawhid • Wonder • Gratitude
missions.aim: Notice creation as signs of Allah’s power while remembering His promise to believers.
missions.tafsir: After warning against rejection, the surah gives hope to believers who do righteous deeds: gardens of delight await them by Allah’s true promise. It then turns our attention to the heavens, mountains, animals, rain and plant life. These are created by Allah, and the passage challenges those who worship beings besides Him to identify what those beings have created. This is a statement of Tawhid and Allah’s sole creative power, not merely a nature-appreciation lesson. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari connect the signs in creation to Allah’s unique right to be worshipped. Children may observe patterns in the natural world and study science, but should not turn a simple drawing into a claim that every scientific question has been fully answered by one verse. The lesson is to appreciate the signs, ask thoughtful questions and remember that creation and provision ultimately belong to Allah.
missions.story: After a rainy afternoon, Imaan and Akhlaq stepped into the garden with Dadi Jaan. Tiny green shoots had appeared where the soil had looked empty the week before. Akhlaq found a snail under a damp leaf, and Imaan watched rainwater move along the garden path. “So many living things,” Akhlaq said. At home he drew the clouds, mountains and plants he had noticed. Sheikh Uncle showed them the verses in Surah Luqman that speak of Allah’s creation and rain. “What you see is not just a collection of pretty things,” he explained. “It reminds you of the One who created and provides.” The children thanked Allah, then carefully returned the snail to its shaded place instead of carrying it away.
missions.question: What do the signs in nature remind a believer?
missions.feedback: Observation and gratitude can work together without pretending we know everything.
missions.action: Notice one living thing outside today and thank Allah for His creation.
missions.reflection: What did I discover when I looked more carefully?
missions.vocabulary: Tawhid — worshipping Allah alone; Ni‘mah — blessing
missions.careNote: No depictions of Allah; separate illustrated nature observations from scientific claims and revelation. Paradise must not be shown as a guaranteed literal rendering.
missions.next: The surah now introduces Luqman, a man granted wisdom.
missions.review: Complete a three-part observation journal: “I saw…”, “I wondered…”, “I thank Allah for…”.

missions.title: Luqman’s First Treasure: Gratitude

ayahs.arabic: وَلَقَدْ ءَاتَيْنَا لُقْمَـٰنَ ٱلْحِكْمَةَ أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ ۚ وَمَن يَشْكُرْ فَإِنَّمَا يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِۦ ۖ وَمَن كَفَرَ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَنِىٌّ حَمِيدٌ  ﴿12﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah gave Luqman wisdom and directed him toward gratitude; whoever is thankful benefits himself, while Allah needs nothing.

options: Care for them and share when appropriate.
Complain until a bigger set appears.
Throw them away once they are used.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:12–12  |  CORE TRAITS: Hikmah • Gratitude • Humility
missions.aim: Understand that wisdom is linked to being grateful to Allah, not merely knowing many facts.
missions.tafsir: Allah says He granted Luqman wisdom and instructed him to give thanks. Gratitude benefits the grateful person; Allah is independent of all need and is worthy of praise. Classical Tafsir treats Luqman as a wise servant, with scholarly discussion about aspects of his biography. The Qur’an itself does not invite us to invent his appearance, a named hometown or unreported dialogue. Wisdom here includes recognising the Giver and using blessings rightly. For children, gratitude means more than saying “thank you” after receiving a gift. It includes using knowledge honestly, caring for possessions, acknowledging parents and teachers, and remembering Allah. But we must not turn the story into “if you thank Allah you will always get more toys tomorrow.” Allah’s wisdom is greater than our immediate preferences, and gratitude remains meaningful in ease as well as difficulty.
missions.story: Akhlaq received a new set of coloured pencils and immediately asked when he could get a larger set. Imaan pointed out that the pencils were already enough for the class poster. She did not call him greedy; she simply invited him to use what he had. They spent the afternoon designing a sign welcoming new students to Amanpur school. When the last colour was added, Akhlaq looked at the finished poster and said, “I nearly forgot how useful this gift is.” At dinner Salaam spoke about Luqman’s wisdom and the Qur’an’s invitation to gratitude. Akhlaq decided to look after his pencils, share them with a classmate who had forgotten theirs, and thank Allah without waiting for another present.
missions.question: Which choice shows gratitude for a new set of pencils?
missions.feedback: True gratitude is felt, spoken and expressed through responsible use.
missions.action: Take care of one blessing you already have and thank Allah for it.
missions.reflection: Which blessing can I use more responsibly today?
missions.careNote: Do not portray Luqman with invented physical features or attribute fictional sayings to him. Respect varied household incomes.
missions.next: Luqman’s next advice begins with the most important foundation: worship Allah alone.
missions.review: Select which of three responses to a gift is grateful, wasteful, or unkind.

missions.title: The Most Important Advice: Worship Allah Alone

ayahs.arabic: وَإِذْ قَالَ لُقْمَـٰنُ لِٱبْنِهِۦ وَهُوَ يَعِظُهُۥ يَـٰبُنَىَّ لَا تُشْرِكْ بِٱللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّ ٱلشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ  ﴿13﴾
ayahs.meaning: Luqman lovingly counselled his son never to associate partners with Allah, for shirk is a tremendous wrong.

options: Worship belongs to Allah alone.
Everything we enjoy should be worshipped.
Respect means hiding what the Qur’an teaches.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:13–13  |  CORE TRAITS: Tawhid • Sincerity • Faith
missions.aim: Learn Luqman’s loving counsel to his son about Tawhid and the seriousness of shirk.
missions.tafsir: Luqman addresses his son with affection: “O my son,” and warns him not to associate partners with Allah. The verse calls shirk a tremendous injustice. This is the theological heart of the teaching, and it must be stated clearly rather than replaced by a generic lesson about kindness. Only Allah is to be worshipped, supplicated to as God, and regarded as the sole Creator and Lord. At the same time, children should not be trained to insult others or accuse classmates of disbelief through casual games. Classical Tafsir stresses the severity of shirk because it gives the rights of the Creator to what cannot deserve them. A child-facing lesson can combine clarity in belief with kindness in speech: a Muslim should be confident about Tawhid and respectful when explaining it. We do not invent further advice as Luqman’s historical words beyond what the Qur’an records.
missions.story: At the school exhibition, Akhlaq was preparing a poster about the things he loved: family, books, football and the stars. He placed a large heading over them all: “Things I am grateful for.” Imaan suggested adding a separate line about the One who made those blessings possible. That evening Sheikh Uncle opened Surah Luqman and explained the advice Luqman gave his son: never associate partners with Allah. “We may love and appreciate many people and things,” he said, “but worship belongs to Allah alone.” Akhlaq carefully rewrote the poster. He wanted his classmates to understand that gratitude toward Allah makes him kinder to people and more careful with the world—not rude to those who think differently.
missions.question: What does Tawhid teach a Muslim child?
missions.feedback: We can explain our belief clearly, gently and without insulting anyone.
missions.action: In your own words, tell a parent or teacher one reason you thank and worship Allah alone.
missions.reflection: How can sincere belief in Allah make me kinder and more truthful?
missions.vocabulary: Shirk — associating partners with Allah; Tawhid — oneness of Allah in worship
missions.careNote: Theological content must remain explicit. No role-play of idolatrous rituals, denunciation contests or attacks on children from other backgrounds.
missions.next: After Tawhid, the surah gives an important teaching about parents.
missions.review: Complete: “I worship Allah alone because…” in a child-friendly text or voice note kept local.

missions.title: Honor Parents, Keep the Right Boundaries

ayahs.arabic: وَوَصَّيْنَا ٱلْإِنسَـٰنَ بِوَٰلِدَيْهِ حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُۥ وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍ وَفِصَـٰلُهُۥ فِى عَامَيْنِ أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِى وَلِوَٰلِدَيْكَ إِلَىَّ ٱلْمَصِيرُ  ﴿14﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah commands gratitude and good treatment toward parents, especially recalling a mother’s hardship during pregnancy and nursing; all return to Him.

ayahs.arabic: وَإِن جَـٰهَدَاكَ عَلَىٰٓ أَن تُشْرِكَ بِى مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلْمٌ فَلَا تُطِعْهُمَا ۖ وَصَاحِبْهُمَا فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا مَعْرُوفًا ۖ وَٱتَّبِعْ سَبِيلَ مَنْ أَنَابَ إِلَىَّ ۚ ثُمَّ إِلَىَّ مَرْجِعُكُمْ فَأُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ  ﴿15﴾
ayahs.meaning: If parents pressure a person to associate partners with Allah, that demand must not be obeyed; still treat them kindly in worldly matters and follow Allah’s path.

options: Do it because obedience has no limits.
Seek help from a trusted, safe adult.
Tell every classmate, but not a responsible adult.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:14–15  |  CORE TRAITS: Respect • Gratitude • Safe boundaries
missions.aim: Learn to honor parents while remembering that no one should be obeyed in disobedience to Allah.
missions.tafsir: These verses command gratitude to Allah and kindness to parents, highlighting a mother’s hardship through pregnancy and early care. They also establish a principled boundary: if parents pressure someone to commit shirk, that command must not be followed, while good companionship in ordinary worldly life continues. Scholars emphasize both religious loyalty and respectful treatment, not harshness or abandonment. A child’s everyday example can be helping at home, speaking respectfully and appreciating caregivers. At the same time, no one should interpret this passage to require a child to accept abuse, dangerous instructions or secrecy about harm. A child may seek trusted adult support and protection, even when the person causing fear is a family member. The lesson must acknowledge children in foster, single-parent or other family arrangements without suggesting that they have less worth. This is a teaching about gratitude and firm moral boundaries.
missions.story: Salamah returned home tired after a long day. Akhlaq noticed that the shoes near the door were scattered and the water jug was empty. He began to help before being asked. Imaan joined him, and together they prepared a quiet place for their mother to rest. Later a classmate asked Akhlaq, “Must a child obey every instruction from an adult?” He remembered Sheikh Uncle’s lesson and answered, “We should respect our parents, but nobody should ask us to do what Allah forbids or to accept danger.” Their teacher agreed and showed the class how to find a trusted adult when a situation feels unsafe. Akhlaq felt grateful for his family and understood that genuine respect does not mean losing the right to ask for protection.
missions.question: An adult asks a child to do something clearly unsafe and keep it secret. What is wise?
missions.feedback: Respect and safety belong together; no one has unlimited authority over a child.
missions.action: Offer one helpful, age-appropriate act of care to a parent or caregiver today.
missions.reflection: How can I show gratitude to a caregiver while knowing when to ask for help?
missions.vocabulary: Birr al-walidayn — dutiful kindness to parents; Ma‘ruf — what is good and proper
missions.careNote: Critical safeguard: no child-blaming, no coerced disclosures, no suggestion to remain in danger. Sensitively include diverse caregiving arrangements.
missions.next: The next advice teaches that even the smallest deed matters to Allah.
missions.review: Sort examples into “kind help,” “ask a question,” and “tell a trusted adult for safety.”

missions.title: The Mustard Seed That Matters

ayahs.arabic: يَـٰبُنَىَّ إِنَّهَآ إِن تَكُ مِثْقَالَ حَبَّةٍ مِّنْ خَرْدَلٍ فَتَكُن فِى صَخْرَةٍ أَوْ فِى ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ أَوْ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ يَأْتِ بِهَا ٱللَّهُ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَطِيفٌ خَبِيرٌ  ﴿16﴾
ayahs.meaning: Luqman explains that Allah knows and will bring forth even a deed as tiny as a mustard seed, wherever hidden; He is Subtle and Fully Aware.

options: Keep it because no one knows.
Return it or give it to a responsible adult.
Hide it to test whether others notice.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:16–16  |  CORE TRAITS: Accountability • Sincerity • Hope
missions.aim: Understand that Allah knows even very small hidden deeds, both good and wrong.
missions.tafsir: Luqman teaches his son that even something the weight of a mustard seed, hidden inside a rock or anywhere in creation, will be brought forth by Allah. The Qur’anic picture emphasizes Allah’s complete knowledge and subtle awareness; no deed escapes Him. The lesson is not that a child should live in fear of invisible surveillance or believe every accident is a sin. Scholars connect this verse with accountability for actions before Allah. We must keep both sides of the lesson: hidden good deeds have value, and hidden wrongdoing should be corrected through repentance and making amends. Children need reassurance that mistakes can be admitted and repaired. For younger learners, a mustard seed is a helpful real-world illustration of smallness; it should not turn the verse into a magical story about a talking seed or an invented account from Luqman’s lifetime.
missions.story: During break time Akhlaq found a small eraser beneath a desk. It would have been easy to slip it into his pocket; nobody else was near. Then he remembered the tiny mustard seed from the Qur’an lesson. He placed the eraser on the teacher’s table with a note saying where he had found it. The next day Mohsin came looking for it and thanked him. Akhlaq was pleased, though he had not expected a reward. Later he accidentally knocked over a class pencil holder. He told the teacher and helped put everything back. Imaan reminded him that Allah knows both the honesty no one sees and the courage it takes to admit a mistake. Small actions, she said, can reveal a very big choice.
missions.question: Nobody sees you find a lost eraser. What should you do?
missions.feedback: Allah knows what is hidden; honesty matters even without an audience.
missions.action: Do one small good deed privately today without asking for praise.
missions.reflection: Which small act of honesty matters even when nobody notices?
missions.careNote: Avoid anxiety, scrupulosity and guilt loops. Reward sincere repair after mistakes; no public disclosure of personal wrongs.
missions.next: Luqman next explains how Salah and helping others belong together.
missions.review: Complete a small-deed sorting exercise: secret kindness, accidental mistake, deliberate dishonesty, honest repair.

missions.title: My Meeting with Allah: Salah

ayahs.arabic: يَـٰبُنَىَّ أَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَأْمُرْ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ وَٱنْهَ عَنِ ٱلْمُنكَرِ وَٱصْبِرْ عَلَىٰ مَآ أَصَابَكَ ۖ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ مِنْ عَزْمِ ٱلْأُمُورِ  ﴿17﴾
ayahs.meaning: Luqman tells his son to establish Salah, encourage what is right, discourage wrong, and patiently endure difficulties: these are matters of firm resolve.

options: Treat prayer as a real act of worship to learn and practise.
Tap a prayer animation instead of offering Salah.
Ignore prayer whenever games are exciting.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:17–17  |  CORE TRAITS: Salah • Consistency • Worship
missions.aim: Learn that establishing Salah means treating it as a regular act of worship and learning to perform it properly.
missions.tafsir: Luqman’s advice in 31:17 begins with “Establish Salah.” Classical exegetes understand this as more than saying a quick phrase: prayer is established with its conditions, prescribed acts and proper times. This connects directly to our separate Imaan & Akhlaq Salah Journey. Child learners can begin with preparation, Wudu, posture names, short recitations and guided practice appropriate to their age, while their family or teachers supervise formal worship. The verse also continues to encouraging right, discouraging wrong and patience, which will receive the next lesson. Avoid claiming that a child who misses a practice session has lost Allah’s love, and do not treat an animation as a religious substitute for real prayer. The purpose of gamification is to support understanding and consistency, not to assign a score to a child’s faith.
missions.story: Akhlaq wanted to rush through his afternoon plan because a football game would begin soon. He found Imaan carefully checking the prayer-time chart. “Could you show me how the two-rak'ah learning practice works?” he asked. She opened their supervised Salah learning activity and helped him review the order of standing, bowing and prostration. Then Salaam guided them through the real prayer at its proper time. Afterwards Akhlaq joined the football game feeling calmer. “I thought preparing for prayer would take away the fun,” he told his father. Salaam smiled. “Learning to give worship its place can help you organise all the other good things in your day.” Akhlaq marked the lesson complete, not because the app had performed Salah for him, but because he had learned a little more about worship.
missions.question: What does the lesson “establish Salah” encourage?
missions.feedback: The app teaches the steps; real Salah is learned and offered with appropriate guidance.
missions.action: With a parent or teacher, practise one part of Salah carefully today.
missions.reflection: How can I make a real place for Salah in my routine?
missions.vocabulary: Iqamat al-salah — establishing prayer; Khushu‘ — attentive humility
missions.careNote: Fiqh differences must follow approved family/teacher settings; never assign legal accountability by app age alone or require proof photos.
missions.next: The same ayah also speaks about helping society and remaining patient.
missions.review: Arrange three Salah positions in the proper sequence using cards.

missions.title: Encourage Good with Wisdom and Patience

ayahs.arabic: يَـٰبُنَىَّ أَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَأْمُرْ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ وَٱنْهَ عَنِ ٱلْمُنكَرِ وَٱصْبِرْ عَلَىٰ مَآ أَصَابَكَ ۖ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ مِنْ عَزْمِ ٱلْأُمُورِ  ﴿17﴾
ayahs.meaning: Luqman tells his son to establish Salah, encourage what is right, discourage wrong, and patiently endure difficulties: these are matters of firm resolve.

options: Humiliate the friend publicly.
Invite inclusion politely and seek teacher help if needed.
Ignore a child who may be unsafe.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:17–17  |  CORE TRAITS: Courage • Gentle advice • Sabr  |  SECOND APPLICATION OF VERSE 17
missions.aim: Practise encouraging good without shaming, bullying or taking unsafe risks.
missions.ayahNote: Verse 31:17 is intentionally revisited here after Mission 8. The original Qur’anic verse remains one complete ayah.
missions.tafsir: The second part of 31:17 urges encouraging what is recognised as right, discouraging wrong and enduring difficulties patiently. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the firmness required to follow these commands, particularly when good advice meets resistance. This does not make children miniature judges of other people’s private conduct. Good counsel needs knowledge, gentleness, appropriate authority and wisdom. A child who sees danger should seek adult help rather than confront a harmful person alone. For everyday learning, choose safe, ordinary moments: inviting a friend to include a classmate, reminding someone gently about returning an item, or supporting a fair classroom rule. Patience does not mean permitting abuse, and choosing a gentle tone does not mean hiding the truth. This mission deliberately returns to the same ayah after the Salah lesson because Luqman placed worship, responsibility and patience together.
missions.story: At lunchtime, two students began leaving a younger child out of their game. Akhlaq wanted to shout at them, but Imaan asked him to pause. She went over and said, “Could we make two teams so everyone gets a turn?” One student rolled his eyes, and Akhlaq felt angry. They did not begin an argument. Instead, they asked the teacher to help organize a fair game. Later Sheikh Uncle explained that Luqman advised his son to encourage good and remain patient. “Patience is not silent approval of wrongdoing,” he said. “It is choosing a wise response instead of losing control.” Akhlaq saw that a gentle invitation, followed by responsible adult help, had done more than shouting would have achieved.
missions.question: A friend excludes another child from a game. What response best fits the lesson?
missions.feedback: Good advice is truthful, gentle and aware of safety and responsibility.
missions.action: Invite someone to join a safe shared activity today.
missions.reflection: How can I encourage good without embarrassing someone?
missions.vocabulary: Ma‘ruf — recognized good; Munkar — wrong; Sabr — patient firmness
missions.careNote: Never pressure children to confront adults, dangerous classmates, or wrongdoing beyond their capacity. No punitive peer policing.
missions.next: Luqman now teaches how humility shows in our face, walk and voice.
missions.review: Choose a calm sentence to invite a classmate into a group activity.

missions.title: A Gentle Face and a Gentle Voice

ayahs.arabic: وَلَا تُصَعِّرْ خَدَّكَ لِلنَّاسِ وَلَا تَمْشِ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ مَرَحًا ۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ كُلَّ مُخْتَالٍ فَخُورٍ  ﴿18﴾
ayahs.meaning: Do not turn away from people contemptuously or walk the earth boastfully; Allah does not love arrogant pride.

ayahs.arabic: وَٱقْصِدْ فِى مَشْيِكَ وَٱغْضُضْ مِن صَوْتِكَ ۚ إِنَّ أَنكَرَ ٱلْأَصْوَٰتِ لَصَوْتُ ٱلْحَمِيرِ  ﴿19﴾
ayahs.meaning: Be balanced in your walk and moderate your voice; harsh, boastful noise is condemned by a vivid comparison.

options: Refuse to listen to anyone else.
Share your work and kindly invite others to speak.
Make a classmate feel small to look important.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:18–19  |  CORE TRAITS: Humility • Respect • Self-control
missions.aim: Learn to treat people without arrogance and to speak in a balanced, respectful way.
missions.tafsir: Luqman warns his son not to turn his cheek away from people in contempt or stride across the earth proudly. He calls for moderation in walking and voice, and strongly criticizes harsh, arrogant loudness using a vivid comparison. Ibn Kathir and al-Munir explain the themes of humility, dignity and appropriate speech. The verse does not teach that people who speak loudly because of disability, a hearing need or an emergency are morally bad. Nor should it be turned into a rule that children must speak softly while facing danger. A respectful child can speak confidently, ask questions and call for help when necessary. The Qur’anic criticism is of boastfulness, contempt and needlessly harsh speech. The safe application is greeting others warmly, listening, avoiding a superior attitude and adjusting one’s voice to the situation.
missions.story: Akhlaq entered the classroom proud of his science model. When Mohsin tried to tell him about his own project, Akhlaq glanced away and continued announcing how amazing his model was. Later Imaan asked, “Did you notice that Mohsin stopped speaking?” Akhlaq felt embarrassed. She helped him rehearse a kinder way to share his excitement: “I am happy with my project. Tell me about yours too.” The next morning he greeted Mohsin, faced him politely and listened. At the assembly he still spoke loudly enough for everyone to hear, but he did not shout at anyone. In the evening Sheikh Uncle explained Luqman’s advice about modest conduct and a balanced voice. Akhlaq realized humility was not hiding his abilities; it was leaving room for others to be heard.
missions.question: You are proud of your school project. What is a humble response?
missions.feedback: Humility means respecting others, not pretending you have no talents.
missions.action: Listen fully to one person today without interrupting or turning away.
missions.reflection: Did I make room for another person to be heard?
missions.careNote: Audio/accessibility rule: distinguish arrogance from disability-related voice needs, public speaking or urgent calls for help.
missions.next: After Luqman’s counsel, the surah returns to Allah’s visible and hidden blessings.
missions.review: Choose an appropriate voice setting for a classroom conversation, assembly and safety emergency.

missions.title: Blessings Seen and Unseen

ayahs.arabic: أَلَمْ تَرَوْا۟ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ سَخَّرَ لَكُم مَّا فِى ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَأَسْبَغَ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعَمَهُۥ ظَـٰهِرَةً وَبَاطِنَةً ۗ وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يُجَـٰدِلُ فِى ٱللَّهِ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ وَلَا هُدًى وَلَا كِتَـٰبٍ مُّنِيرٍ  ﴿20﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah has made creation beneficial to people and surrounded them with visible and hidden blessings; some still argue without knowledge or revelation.

ayahs.arabic: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمُ ٱتَّبِعُوا۟ مَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ قَالُوا۟ بَلْ نَتَّبِعُ مَا وَجَدْنَا عَلَيْهِ ءَابَآءَنَآ ۚ أَوَلَوْ كَانَ ٱلشَّيْطَـٰنُ يَدْعُوهُمْ إِلَىٰ عَذَابِ ٱلسَّعِيرِ  ﴿21﴾
ayahs.meaning: When called to follow what Allah revealed, some refuse and insist blindly on ancestral habits, even where those habits lead to error.

ayahs.arabic: وَمَن يُسْلِمْ وَجْهَهُۥٓ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ فَقَدِ ٱسْتَمْسَكَ بِٱلْعُرْوَةِ ٱلْوُثْقَىٰ ۗ وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ عَـٰقِبَةُ ٱلْأُمُورِ  ﴿22﴾
ayahs.meaning: Whoever submits sincerely to Allah while doing good holds firmly to the most secure support; every matter returns to Allah.

options: Mock the friend’s family.
Ask respectfully for evidence and guidance.
Declare all family customs forbidden.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:20–22  |  CORE TRAITS: Gratitude • Evidence • Steadfastness
missions.aim: Recognize Allah’s blessings and follow revelation instead of copying harmful customs blindly.
missions.tafsir: Allah reminds people of benefits throughout the heavens and earth, including blessings apparent and not immediately visible. The verses then challenge argument without knowledge, guidance or illuminating scripture. Some reject revelation merely because they found a different practice among their forefathers. The surah teaches that sincere submission to Allah together with good conduct is a firm handhold. Classical Tafsir connects this to sound belief and to refusing to make ancestral custom the final authority when it contradicts revelation. For a child, the lesson should not become contempt for elders or culture: many family customs are good or permissible. The key is to distinguish religious evidence from habit and to ask respectfully when unsure. The “firm handhold” is a Qur’anic image of security in faith, not a magical object that can be collected in a game.
missions.story: During an Amanpur school project, each student was asked to share a family habit. Akhlaq described how his family greeted guests and offered them water. Mohsina shared another welcoming custom from her home. Everyone enjoyed learning. Later someone claimed that a particular classroom tradition was compulsory in Islam simply because their grandparents had always done it. Imaan suggested they ask the teacher for evidence before making a religious claim. Sheikh Uncle helped the children distinguish between a lovely local custom and an act Allah has commanded. He also asked them to list blessings they often overlook, such as clean water, safety and helpful friends. Akhlaq discovered that honoring family and following revelation can go together, provided neither habit nor pride takes the place of knowledge.
missions.question: A friend says a family habit is compulsory in Islam only because it is old. What should you do?
missions.feedback: Respect people and traditions while checking religious claims against sound guidance.
missions.action: Thank Allah for one everyday blessing you usually overlook.
missions.reflection: Which family custom is lovely, and which religious claim needs evidence?
missions.vocabulary: Ni‘mah zahirah — visible blessing; Istimsak — holding firmly
missions.careNote: Never treat the metaphor of the firm handhold as a literal mystical object. Do not ridicule families or local cultural traditions.
missions.next: The surah reminds the Prophet ﷺ that people’s responses ultimately return to Allah.
missions.review: Sort six cards into evidence, ordinary cultural practice and unsupported religious claim.

missions.title: The Truth Is Not a Popularity Contest

ayahs.arabic: وَمَن كَفَرَ فَلَا يَحْزُنكَ كُفْرُهُۥٓ ۚ إِلَيْنَا مَرْجِعُهُمْ فَنُنَبِّئُهُم بِمَا عَمِلُوٓا۟ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌۢ بِذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُورِ  ﴿23﴾
ayahs.meaning: The disbelief of others should not overwhelm the Messenger ﷺ; all will return to Allah, Who knows the secrets of hearts.

ayahs.arabic: نُمَتِّعُهُمْ قَلِيلًا ثُمَّ نَضْطَرُّهُمْ إِلَىٰ عَذَابٍ غَلِيظٍ  ﴿24﴾
ayahs.meaning: The present enjoyment of this world is brief, and the verse warns that rejecting truth carries consequences.

ayahs.arabic: وَلَئِن سَأَلْتَهُم مَّنْ خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ لَيَقُولُنَّ ٱللَّهُ ۚ قُلِ ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ ۚ بَلْ أَكْثَرُهُمْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ  ﴿25﴾
ayahs.meaning: Even those questioned about creation acknowledge that Allah created the heavens and earth; praise belongs to Him, though many do not understand.

ayahs.arabic: لِلَّهِ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلْغَنِىُّ ٱلْحَمِيدُ  ﴿26﴾
ayahs.meaning: Everything in the heavens and on earth belongs to Allah; He is Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy.

options: Insult them until they agree.
Remain truthful and respectful; you cannot control hearts.
Change every belief just to be popular.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:23–26  |  CORE TRAITS: Sincerity • Patience • Accountability
missions.aim: Learn that Allah knows hearts and owns creation even when people reject true guidance.
missions.tafsir: Verses 23–26 address the reality that some reject revelation. The Prophet ﷺ is told not to be overwhelmed by their disbelief; they will return to Allah, Who knows what is hidden in hearts. The passage warns that worldly enjoyment is brief and notes that even those questioned about the origin of the heavens and earth acknowledge Allah as Creator. Everything belongs to Allah, the Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy. This theological statement must not be reduced to “ignore everyone who disagrees.” A child can discuss beliefs courteously and continue doing what is right without trying to control the beliefs of peers. Matters of punishment and the Hereafter should be explained in calm, truthful, adult-supported language rather than scary game effects. The point is the certainty of Allah’s knowledge and the responsibility to remain faithful, not to label other children as doomed.
missions.story: Akhlaq had prepared a short school presentation about gratitude to Allah. A few classmates were interested; others preferred another topic. He was disappointed because he had hoped everyone would agree with him. Salaam listened and said that speaking with kindness matters more than winning everyone’s approval. At their lesson, Sheikh Uncle explained that Surah Luqman reminds us Allah knows what is in hearts, and we cannot force other people to believe what we believe. Imaan helped Akhlaq improve his presentation so it included clear ideas and respectful responses to questions. On the presentation day he spoke sincerely, thanked those who listened, and remained kind to those who chose not to participate. His responsibility was to speak truthfully and act well, not to control anyone’s heart.
missions.question: People disagree with your presentation. What is the best response?
missions.feedback: Sincere faith is not measured by applause or agreement from everyone.
missions.action: Speak respectfully to one person who has a different preference today.
missions.reflection: How do I behave when people disagree with me?
missions.careNote: No visual punishment scenes or classifying children as believers/disbelievers. Keep the Qur’anic theological meaning explicit without cruelty.
missions.next: The next verses remind us how immense Allah’s knowledge and power are.
missions.review: Build a courteous two-sentence response to a disagreement.

missions.title: More Than All the Ink in the Sea

ayahs.arabic: وَلَوْ أَنَّمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ مِن شَجَرَةٍ أَقْلَـٰمٌ وَٱلْبَحْرُ يَمُدُّهُۥ مِنۢ بَعْدِهِۦ سَبْعَةُ أَبْحُرٍ مَّا نَفِدَتْ كَلِمَـٰتُ ٱللَّهِ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ  ﴿27﴾
ayahs.meaning: If all trees became pens and many seas became ink, Allah’s words would not run out; He is Mighty and Wise.

ayahs.arabic: مَّا خَلْقُكُمْ وَلَا بَعْثُكُمْ إِلَّا كَنَفْسٍ وَٰحِدَةٍ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ سَمِيعٌۢ بَصِيرٌ  ﴿28﴾
ayahs.meaning: Creating and resurrecting everyone is no harder for Allah than creating and resurrecting a single soul; He hears and sees all.

ayahs.arabic: أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُولِجُ ٱلَّيْلَ فِى ٱلنَّهَارِ وَيُولِجُ ٱلنَّهَارَ فِى ٱلَّيْلِ وَسَخَّرَ ٱلشَّمْسَ وَٱلْقَمَرَ كُلٌّ يَجْرِىٓ إِلَىٰٓ أَجَلٍ مُّسَمًّى وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرٌ  ﴿29﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah causes day and night to overlap, and directs the sun and moon on appointed courses; He knows everything people do.

options: Allah’s words and knowledge are beyond human limits.
Children should stop studying because they cannot learn everything.
There are exactly seven scientific oceans in the world.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:27–29  |  CORE TRAITS: Knowledge • Wonder • Humility
missions.aim: Appreciate the vastness of Allah’s words and knowledge while learning responsibly about the world.
missions.tafsir: Verse 27 imagines every tree as a pen and the sea enlarged by seven more seas of ink. Even then, the words of Allah would not be exhausted. Verse 28 affirms Allah’s power over creation and resurrection, and verse 29 points to the passage of night and day and the courses of the sun and moon. Classical interpreters treat these images as demonstrations of Allah’s unlimited power and knowledge. The “seven seas” is a Qur’anic expression in this verse; we should not teach it as a scientific census of literal oceans. Likewise, day/night and celestial movements invite observation without turning a child’s planet model into a detailed Tafsir proof of modern astronomy. The child may love books and research, but must recognise that human learning is finite. Wonder should lead to humility, not pride in having all the answers.
missions.story: The school library opened a new science corner. Akhlaq tried to count every book on the shelves while Imaan wondered how many more books might be written in the future. They sketched a huge tree filled with pencils and a sea filled with ink. Sheikh Uncle read the verse about all the trees becoming pens and the seas becoming ink. “The image teaches us how far beyond our limits Allah’s words are,” he explained. The children talked about questions scientists can investigate, questions they still cannot answer, and the knowledge Allah possesses perfectly. On the way home they watched the evening sky deepen into darkness. Akhlaq wrote in his journal: “Learning more is exciting, and it reminds me how much I still do not know.”
missions.question: What is the lesson of trees as pens and seas as ink?
missions.action: Ask one thoughtful question about the natural world and look for a reliable answer.
missions.reflection: Which question reminds me that there is more to learn?
missions.vocabulary: Kalimāt Allah — Allah’s words; Ba‘th — resurrection
missions.careNote: Treat the metaphor accurately; do not derive unsupported scientific numerology or assert the seven seas identify seven physical oceans.
missions.next: The surah draws a connection between truth, gratitude and trust during difficulty.
missions.review: Choose whether a statement is an observable fact, a Qur’anic teaching or an unsupported guess.

missions.title: Grateful in Calm and Storm

ayahs.arabic: ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلْحَقُّ وَأَنَّ مَا يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِهِ ٱلْبَـٰطِلُ وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْكَبِيرُ  ﴿30﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah alone is the Truth; objects falsely worshipped besides Him are false, and He is the Most High, the Great.

ayahs.arabic: أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱلْفُلْكَ تَجْرِى فِى ٱلْبَحْرِ بِنِعْمَتِ ٱللَّهِ لِيُرِيَكُم مِّنْ ءَايَـٰتِهِۦٓ ۚ إِنَّ فِى ذَٰلِكَ لَـَٔايَـٰتٍ لِّكُلِّ صَبَّارٍ شَكُورٍ  ﴿31﴾
ayahs.meaning: Ships travel across the sea through Allah’s favour so people may notice His signs; this is meaningful for those who are patient and thankful.

ayahs.arabic: وَإِذَا غَشِيَهُم مَّوْجٌ كَٱلظُّلَلِ دَعَوُا۟ ٱللَّهَ مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ ٱلدِّينَ فَلَمَّا نَجَّىٰهُمْ إِلَى ٱلْبَرِّ فَمِنْهُم مُّقْتَصِدٌ ۚ وَمَا يَجْحَدُ بِـَٔايَـٰتِنَآ إِلَّا كُلُّ خَتَّارٍ كَفُورٍ  ﴿32﴾
ayahs.meaning: When towering waves threaten them, people turn sincerely to Allah; after safety returns, their responses differ, and the verse warns against ungrateful betrayal.

options: Ignore safety rules and take risks.
Follow the teacher’s guidance and remember Allah with gratitude.
Assume bad weather means Allah dislikes you.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:30–32  |  CORE TRAITS: Tawhid • Patience • Gratitude
missions.aim: Understand Allah alone is the Truth and learn to remember Him in both ease and difficulty.
missions.tafsir: Verse 30 reaffirms Tawhid: Allah is the Truth, while what is worshipped besides Him is false. The next verses describe ships moving by Allah’s favour, then people facing waves so high they turn to Him with sincere devotion. After rescue, their responses differ; some remain upright, while others deny His signs. Classical Tafsir treats this contrast as exposing how quickly people may forget their need for Allah once danger passes. A child-facing application should encourage thankfulness after an ordinary difficulty rather than staging frightening shipwreck simulations. It also teaches sensible preparation: trust in Allah is consistent with listening to adults, following weather warnings and taking safety precautions. The Qur’anic imagery about danger remains meaningful without causing anxiety or promising that every storm will end exactly as a child hopes.
missions.story: Amanpur’s school picnic had to move indoors when dark clouds gathered. Akhlaq was disappointed because he had planned outdoor games. The teachers checked the forecast and guided everyone into the hall safely. Soon the students began inventing indoor activities. Akhlaq suggested a puzzle contest and helped a younger child who had been frightened by the thunder. Later, when the weather improved, Imaan thanked Allah for keeping them safe. Sheikh Uncle read the verses about people who call sincerely upon Allah during danger and forget gratitude afterwards. Akhlaq realised that he should remember Allah both when plans go well and when they change. He also learned that making Du'a does not replace taking wise safety precautions.
missions.question: Heavy rain interrupts an outdoor activity. What is the wise response?
missions.feedback: Trust in Allah includes sensible precautions and gratitude in changing circumstances.
missions.action: Say Alhamdulillah after one difficulty eases today, and thank someone who helped.
missions.reflection: What can I remember Allah for after a difficult moment?
missions.careNote: No distressing wave scenes, “disaster caused by bad child” messaging, or promises of safety in exchange for app rewards.
missions.next: The surah closes by reminding each person of accountability and Allah’s full knowledge.
missions.review: Choose a safe rainy-day plan and one sincere gratitude sentence.

missions.title: Tomorrow Belongs to Allah

ayahs.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ٱتَّقُوا۟ رَبَّكُمْ وَٱخْشَوْا۟ يَوْمًا لَّا يَجْزِى وَالِدٌ عَن وَلَدِهِۦ وَلَا مَوْلُودٌ هُوَ جَازٍ عَن وَالِدِهِۦ شَيْـًٔا ۚ إِنَّ وَعْدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقٌّ ۖ فَلَا تَغُرَّنَّكُمُ ٱلْحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنْيَا وَلَا يَغُرَّنَّكُم بِٱللَّهِ ٱلْغَرُورُ  ﴿33﴾
ayahs.meaning: Human beings are called to be mindful of their Lord and the Day when no parent or child can take another’s accountability; worldly life must not deceive them.

ayahs.arabic: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عِندَهُۥ عِلْمُ ٱلسَّاعَةِ وَيُنَزِّلُ ٱلْغَيْثَ وَيَعْلَمُ مَا فِى ٱلْأَرْحَامِ ۖ وَمَا تَدْرِى نَفْسٌ مَّاذَا تَكْسِبُ غَدًا ۖ وَمَا تَدْرِى نَفْسٌۢ بِأَىِّ أَرْضٍ تَمُوتُ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌۢ  ﴿34﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah possesses full knowledge of the Hour, brings down rain, knows what is in wombs, and knows tomorrow’s deeds and the place of death; He is All-Knowing, All-Aware.

options: Say nothing can ever change and make no backup plan.
Prepare well, say “in sha Allah,” and remain flexible.
Refuse to make plans because only Allah knows the future.
missions.anchor: SURAH LUQMAN • 31:33–34  |  CORE TRAITS: Taqwa • Responsibility • Humility about the unseen
missions.aim: Learn to prepare responsibly for tomorrow while recognising Allah’s complete knowledge of the unseen and the Hereafter.
missions.tafsir: The closing verses call all people to be mindful of their Lord and the Day of Return, when each person is accountable before Allah. They warn against being deceived by worldly life. Verse 34 describes matters encompassed by Allah’s perfect knowledge: the Hour, rain, what is in wombs, what a person will earn tomorrow and where a person will die. Classical Tafsir links this to the keys of the unseen and Allah’s complete knowledge. Human observations, forecasts and medical tests can reveal limited details; they do not equal the comprehensive knowledge belonging to Allah. Children should learn to plan, work and say “in sha Allah” with sincerity rather than give up responsibility because the future is unknown. This lesson needs gentle discussion of death and accountability for younger ages; it must never make children fearful of sleep, pregnancy or tomorrow.
missions.story: Akhlaq drew a plan for the next week: homework, Qur’an review, football and time with Dadi Jaan. When a neighbour asked whether the sports day would be sunny, he confidently replied, “It definitely will!” Imaan showed him the forecast and reminded him that forecasts can change. At the family lesson, Sheikh Uncle explained that Allah knows tomorrow perfectly while human beings make their best plans with limited knowledge. Akhlaq crossed out “definitely” and wrote “in sha Allah” beside his plans. He did not stop preparing; he packed his books and checked the timetable. When the week ended differently from his first plan, he adjusted calmly and thanked Allah for the chances he still had to learn and help.
missions.question: You are making plans for tomorrow. What shows both trust and responsibility?
missions.feedback: We act responsibly while recognising that complete knowledge belongs to Allah.
missions.action: Make one simple plan for tomorrow and say “in sha Allah” sincerely.
missions.reflection: What can I plan responsibly while leaving tomorrow to Allah?
missions.vocabulary: Taqwa — mindfulness of Allah; Ghayb — unseen
missions.careNote: Explain 31:34 with care: weather forecasts and prenatal tests are partial human findings, not comprehensive divine knowledge. Gentle, parent-led Hereafter treatment.
missions.next: Our surah journey closes with the promise to choose worship, gratitude and kind conduct each day.
missions.review: Compare a confident prediction, a sensible preparation and a claim of knowing the unseen.
